title: Absence of Spin-Glass Order on Migdal--Kadanoff Hierarchical Lattices near Three Dimensions
summary: We derive a rigorous sufficient condition for the absence of spin-glass order in the Ising spin glass with symmetric binary couplings on Migdal--Kadanoff (MK) hierarchical lattices with even branching number. The key observation is that a single exact renormalization-group step creates zero effective bonds with positive probability, thereby reducing the problem to bond percolation on the corresponding hierarchical lattice. When the induced dilution exceeds the percolation threshold, both spin-glass order and stiffness are absent at all temperatures, including zero temperature. As a consequence, our criterion gives a rigorous proof that the Ising spin glass on the square lattice does not exhibit a spin-glass phase within the MK approximation. More unexpectedly, by choosing sufficiently large scale factors and branching numbers, we construct MK hierarchical lattices whose fractal dimensions are arbitrarily close to three from below but still exhibit no spin-glass order. This sharply contrasts with numerical estimates obtained for MK hierarchical lattices with relatively small scale factors and branching numbers, which placed the lower critical dimension near \(2.52\).

AI.tldr: This paper derives a rigorous sufficient condition for the absence of spin-glass order in Ising spin glasses on Migdal-Kadanoff hierarchical lattices with symmetric binary couplings and even branching numbers, using the observation that a single RG step creates zero effective bonds with positive probability, reducing the problem to bond percolation. The criterion proves no spin-glass phase on the square lattice within the MK approximation and constructs hierarchical lattices with fractal dimensions arbitrarily close to 3 that still lack spin-glass order, contradicting prior numerical estimates placing the lower critical dimension near 2.52.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous criterion for the absence of spin-glass order in Ising spin glasses on MK hierarchical lattices and to resolve discrepancies regarding the lower critical dimension of spin-glass systems.
AI.method: The authors show that a single exact RG step on MK hierarchical lattices with even branching numbers creates zero effective bonds with positive probability. This reduces the problem to bond percolation on the hierarchical lattice. When induced dilution exceeds the percolation threshold, both spin-glass order and stiffness are absent at all temperatures.
AI.result: The criterion proves rigorously that the Ising spin glass on the square lattice has no spin-glass phase within the MK approximation. Moreover, MK hierarchical lattices can be constructed with fractal dimensions arbitrarily close to 3 (from below) that still exhibit no spin-glass order, contradicting prior numerical estimates that placed the lower critical dimension near 2.52.
AI.conclusion: The lower critical dimension for spin-glass order on MK hierarchical lattices is at least 3, or the behavior is not governed solely by fractal dimension but also by other lattice properties.

title: A Flickering Resonance Degeneracy on Entropy-Ruled Charge Transport in the Extended Hopping Sites for Biological Systems: Role of Static-to-Dynamic Disorder Transition
summary: Charge transport (CT) in biological systems is of great interest due to its role in various functional activities like photobiology, bioenergetics, redox catalytic and other metabolic activities, etc. It has been observed by various studies that the presence of a dynamic disorder in biomolecules facilitates charge dynamics in the intermediate transport regime, i.e., far from hopping and towards a bank-like mechanism. Hitherto, the dynamic disorder (in a time scale, coupling between electronic and nuclear dynamics) weightage on CT in molecules is not well-established for the measurement of molecular conductivity from small to long-range ordering. With this motivation, we propose the flickering resonance-coupled entropy-ruled charge transport theory for transfer-rate and diffusion-based mobility (D/μ) calculations. The proposed analytical formalism incorporates the impact of dynamic disorder-correlated degeneracy (in a flickering-resonance manner) on the entropy-ruled electron transfer rate and diffusion-mobility, which are valid for localized hopping, delocalized band transport, and regimes in between. By this approach, it has been observed that the dynamics-driven electronic site matching probability enhances the degeneracy, which is quantified by the differential entropy. The analysis clearly shows that for ultra-fast dynamical and degenerate cases, the entropy-ruled mobility is transformed as band mobility, rather than the thermally activated hopping or diffusion process.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a flickering resonance-coupled entropy-ruled charge transport theory that incorporates dynamic disorder-correlated degeneracy to describe charge transport across regimes from hopping to band-like, showing that in ultra-fast dynamical cases, entropy-ruled mobility transforms into band mobility.
AI.motivation: The weightage of dynamic disorder on charge transport in molecules is not well-established for measuring molecular conductivity across small to long-range ordering, motivating the need for a unified theoretical framework.
AI.method: The authors develop an analytical formalism for transfer-rate and diffusion-based mobility (D/μ) calculations based on flickering resonance-coupled entropy-ruled charge transport theory, incorporating dynamic disorder-correlated degeneracy quantified by differential entropy.
AI.result: The dynamics-driven electronic site matching probability enhances degeneracy as quantified by differential entropy. For ultra-fast dynamical and degenerate cases, entropy-ruled mobility transforms into band mobility rather than thermally activated hopping or diffusion.
AI.conclusion: The proposed theory bridges localized hopping, delocalized band transport, and intermediate regimes, establishing dynamic disorder's role in facilitating charge dynamics through flickering-resonance mechanisms.

title: Quantum and classical entropic complexity of the thermal state: coherence, decoherence, and the ergodic-to-localized crossover in random-matrix and many-body models
summary: Does thermal averaging preserve signatures of eigenstate complexity? We study the entropic complexity C = S_1 - S_2 (Shannon minus second-order Renyi entropy) across the ergodic-to-localized crossover of three disordered models: the Rosenzweig-Porter (RP) ensemble, the power-law banded random matrix (PLBRM) ensemble, and the random-field Heisenberg chain. We compare a wavefunction-level quantity C_eig to the complexity of the thermal (Gibbs) state before and after pointer-basis dephasing, via the trace (C_tr) and diagonal (C_diag) complexities. The answer is mostly no: thermal averaging strongly suppresses, but does not eliminate, eigenstate-complexity signatures. C_eig develops a pronounced mid-phase maximum in RP and, at matching fractal dimension, in the structurally independent PLBRM model; a high-statistics scan resolves a weak (about 10%) but reproducible thermal shadow of this peak in the thermal diagonal complexity. This feature is confined to the two random-matrix models; in the Heisenberg chain the eigenstate complexity instead peaks at the many-body localization transition. A second, genuinely thermal feature, an edge just inside the ergodic phase, has no eigenstate counterpart and, in PLBRM, recedes with system size. Both features are tracked by scale-invariant crossover indicators: the log-ratio of the trace and diagonal crossover temperatures, which vanishes upon localization, and the relative entropy of coherence. Entropic complexity thus cleanly separates thermal-state and eigenstate physics: a sharp wavefunction-level feature, reproducible across unrelated random-matrix constructions, leaves only a faint, structurally distinct imprint on thermal observables.

AI.tldr: Thermal averaging mostly suppresses eigenstate complexity signatures across disordered models, leaving only faint thermal imprints; distinct wavefunction-level features (mid-phase maximum) in random-matrix models are reproducible but barely visible in thermal states.
AI.motivation: To determine whether entropic complexity (Shannon minus second-order Renyi entropy) signatures of eigenstate complexity survive thermal averaging, comparing wavefunction-level (C_eig) with thermal-state complexities (C_tr, C_diag) across three disordered models.
AI.method: Study entropic complexity C = S_1 - S_2 across the ergodic-to-localized crossover in three models: Rosenzweig-Porter (RP) ensemble, power-law banded random matrix (PLBRM) ensemble, and random-field Heisenberg chain. Compare eigenstate complexity C_eig to thermal (Gibbs) state complexity before and after pointer-basis dephasing, using trace (C_tr) and diagonal (C_diag) complexities. Track scale-invariant crossover indicators: log-ratio of trace/diagonal crossover temperatures and relative entropy of coherence.
AI.result: C_eig shows a pronounced mid-phase maximum in RP and PLBRM (at matching fractal dimension); a weak (~10%) but reproducible thermal shadow of this peak appears in C_diag but only in random-matrix models. In the Heisenberg chain, eigenstate complexity peaks at the many-body localization transition. A second, genuinely thermal feature (edge inside ergodic phase) has no eigenstate counterpart and recedes with system size in PLBRM.
AI.conclusion: Thermal averaging strongly suppresses but does not entirely eliminate eigenstate-complexity signatures; entropic complexity cleanly separates thermal-state and eigenstate physics, with sharp wavefunction-level features leaving only faint, structurally distinct imprints on thermal observables.

title: Shielded RL for Route-Charged Parity-Term Ordering in QEDA Phase Components
summary: Commuting phase terms in quantum electronic design automation (QEDA) placement circuits are logically invariant under reordering, yet their routed cost varies substantially after hardware mapping, since term order affects CNOT cancellation, interaction locality, and routing pressure. We cast parity/support phase-term ordering within a QEDA phase component as a shielded reinforcement-learning problem: a feasibility shield restricts each step to unemitted terms, so every trajectory is a valid permutation by construction, and an elite (cross-entropy-method) policy is trained against a route-charged proxy combining support-transition size and heavy-hex topology-distance features. We validate by direct Qiskit routing of logically equivalent circuits to a synthetic IBM-style heavy-hex map. On 36-term parity-walk components (50 term seeds x 2 transpiler seeds, statistics at the term-seed level), the per-instance learned ordering reduces mean routed CX to 336.0, a 5.7-12.2% paired reduction over 2-opt and simulated-annealing search at equal or greater proxy budget and 22.3% over the default construction order; routed-CX and routed-depth gains are significant after Bonferroni correction. Honest transfer audits show the proxy is predictive for the parity-walk component but not for extraction-heavy or token/permutation circuits, which require architecture-aware rewards, scoping the contribution accordingly.

AI.tldr: A reinforcement-learning approach with a feasibility shield optimizes phase-term ordering in QEDA circuits, achieving 5.7-22.3% reduction in routed CNOT count for parity-walk components on heavy-hex hardware.
AI.motivation: Commuting phase terms in QEDA placement circuits have logically invariant order, but term ordering significantly impacts CNOT cancellation, interaction locality, and routing pressure after hardware mapping. The goal is to find optimal term permutations that minimize routed cost.
AI.method: Formulates phase-term ordering as a shielded reinforcement-learning problem: a feasibility shield ensures only unemitted terms are selected (valid permutations by construction). An elite cross-entropy-method policy is trained against a route-charged proxy combining support-transition size and heavy-hex topology-distance features. Validation uses Qiskit routing on synthetic IBM-style heavy-hex maps.
AI.result: On 36-term parity-walk components (50 seeds × 2 transpiler seeds), the learned ordering achieves mean routed CX = 336.0, a 5.7-12.2% reduction over 2-opt and simulated annealing, and 22.3% over default construction order. Gains in routed-CX and routed-depth are significant after Bonferroni correction.
AI.conclusion: The proxy is predictive for parity-walk components but not for extraction-heavy or token/permutation circuits, which require architecture-aware rewards. The contribution is scoped to parity-walk phase components.

title: Structure-Agnostic Unitary Learning from Quantum Observable Dynamics with Application to Hamiltonian Identification
comment: 7 pages, 15 tables, 1 algorithm.This preprint is based on and extends the author's Master's thesis completed at Université Ferhat Abbas Sétif 1 (2026)
summary:
We present a variational algorithm for learning an unknown quantum unitary from time-series observable measurements, with no structural assumption about the target. The core separation: a hardware-efficient parametrised circuit learns the evolution operator U via observable matching; Hamiltonian identification follows as classical post-processing via matrix logarithm, when the target happens to be exp(-iH*tau).
  Three experiments establish the method's generality. First, a noiseless proof of correctness with exact gradients (L-BFGS-B) achieves MSE 1.61e-14 and recovers all Hamiltonian coefficients to six decimal places. Second, a gate-learning experiment fits CNOT, iSWAP, and a Haar-random SU(4) element -- none generated by any fixed Hamiltonian -- all to process fidelity 1.000000, confirming the method does not rely on Trotterisation structure. Third, quantum deployment via SPSA-Adam under Qiskit Aer depolarising noise (p1=0.001, p2=0.01, Nshots=1024) recovers all three Ising Hamiltonian terms with errors below 8%.
  The optimiser, SPSA-Adam, combines SPSA's hardware-efficient two-point gradient estimation with Adam's adaptive moment updates. A four-stage moment-warm curriculum progressively extends the training horizon, converting a global non-convex problem into a sequence of well-posed local ones.

AI.tldr: A variational algorithm learns unknown quantum unitaries from time-series observable measurements via hardware-efficient circuit learning and Hamiltonian identification as classical post-processing, validated through three experiments including noiseless correctness, gate-learning (CNOT, iSWAP, Haar-random SU(4)), and noisy quantum deployment on Ising Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: To learn an unknown quantum unitary from observable measurements without structural assumptions (e.g., no Trotterisation or Hamiltonian structure required), enabling both black-box unitary learning and subsequent Hamiltonian identification.
AI.method: A hardware-efficient parametrised circuit learns the evolution operator U via observable matching; Hamiltonian coefficients are recovered via classical matrix logarithm post-processing. The optimizer is SPSA-Adam, combining SPSA's two-point gradient estimation with Adam's adaptive moments, aided by a four-stage moment-warm curriculum that converts the global non-convex problem into local convex subproblems.
AI.result: (1) Noiseless: MSE 1.61e-14, Hamiltonian coefficients recovered to 6 decimal places. (2) Gate-learning: CNOT, iSWAP, and Haar-random SU(4) all achieve process fidelity 1.000000. (3) Noisy quantum deployment (Qiskit Aer, p1=0.001, p2=0.01, Nshots=1024): all three Ising Hamiltonian terms recovered with errors below 8%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed variational method can learn arbitrary quantum unitaries (including those not generated by any fixed Hamiltonian) from measurement data alone, and perform Hamiltonian identification as a downstream classical task, with robustness to realistic noise levels.

title: Collective Enhancement of Nuclear Excitation for a Nuclear Quantum Battery
summary: Current implementations of quantum batteries are constrained by limited energy density and short retention times associated with the electronic or molecular excitations. Here we propose a nuclear quantum battery based on collective excitation of the $^{57}$Fe nuclei of density $n$ embedded in a planar hard X-ray waveguide. Using a Green function waveguide-QED description, we study charging via excitation beyond linear response, where saturation and drive back-action reshape the incident pulse. We introduce a self-consistent waveform-engineering protocol that inhibits local radiative decay in the waveguide thus promoting absorption into high-lying collective nuclear excitation manifolds. We show an enhanced excitation cross section of the nuclear ensemble which yields superlinear charging, with maximum studied energy density scaling approximately like $n \sqrt{n}$. Our results provide a route to high-energy-density quantum charging at hard X-ray energies using contemporary X-ray sources and waveguide architectures by identifying nonlinear, collectively enhanced absorption as a key mechanism for nuclear quantum battery operation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a nuclear quantum battery using 57Fe nuclei in an X-ray waveguide, achieving superlinear charging and high energy density via collective excitation and a waveform-engineering protocol that suppresses radiative decay.
AI.motivation: Current quantum batteries suffer from low energy density and short retention times due to reliance on electronic or molecular excitations, motivating the need for a more stable, high-density energy storage system.
AI.method: The authors use a Green function waveguide-QED description to model charging beyond linear response, and introduce a self-consistent waveform-engineering protocol that inhibits local radiative decay in the waveguide, promoting absorption into high-lying collective nuclear excitation manifolds.
AI.result: The nuclear ensemble exhibits an enhanced excitation cross section yielding superlinear charging, with maximum studied energy density scaling approximately like n√n, where n is the nuclear density.
AI.conclusion: Collectively enhanced nonlinear absorption provides a viable route to high-energy-density quantum charging at hard X-ray energies using contemporary X-ray sources and waveguide architectures.

title: Quantum error-correcting codes from aperiodic monotiles: the Hat and the Spectre
summary: Li and Boyle showed that the Penrose tiling defines a quantum error-correcting code: superpositions of tilings over isometry orbits protect quantum information against erasure of any bounded region. We extend the construction to the aperiodic monotiles discovered by Smith, Myers, Kaplan and Goodman-Strauss. For the Hat, we prove strong local indistinguishability for all Hat tilings, and we prove local recoverability unconditionally for all nonsingular Hat tilings via the torus parametrization of the underlying cut-and-project scheme. The remaining singular case reduces to one sharply posed geometric question -- can a region that is a union of hats be retiled a second way? -- which we verify computationally has no counterexample up to a substantial scale: a certified $2490$-tile patch admits precisely one tiling by hats, so all $2^{2490}$ of its tile-subregions retile uniquely. Unlike the Penrose, Ammann-Beenker and Fibonacci tilings, both monotiles form two local-indistinguishability classes, so their code spaces split into two erasure-correcting sectors carrying a superselected classical label. Whether the label survives depends on which isometries are gauged: the Spectre's classes are exchanged by a $30^{\circ}$ rotation and merge once all proper isometries are gauged, whereas the Hat's are exchanged only by reflections. Under the physically natural gauge group $SE(2)$, the Hat code therefore stores one robust classical bit -- the handedness of its long-range order, readable in any bounded window with separation $Δ= |K|\sqrt{5}/3$ -- alongside its protected quantum sectors. It is the reflexible monotile, not the chiral one, that carries the chirality bit. We give the exact Perron-Frobenius data of both codes, including the per-class reflected-Hat frequencies $(3\mp\sqrt{5})/6$ and the Spectre orientation-class frequencies $(5\pm\sqrt{15})/10$.

AI.tldr: The paper extends quantum error-correcting codes from Penrose tilings to aperiodic monotiles (Hat and Spectre), proving local indistinguishability, local recoverability, and identifying two erasure-correcting sectors with a superselected classical bit arising from the Hat's chirality under the SE(2) gauge group.
AI.motivation: To generalize the Penrose tiling quantum error-correcting code construction to recently discovered aperiodic monotiles (Hat and Spectre), investigating how their structural properties affect code capacity, local recoverability, and classical information storage.
AI.method: Extends the isometry-orbit superposition framework from Penrose tilings to monotiles; uses torus parametrization from cut-and-project schemes for local recoverability; classifies tilings by local indistinguishability classes; computes Perron-Frobenius data for frequency distributions; verifies unique retiling via certified computational search.
AI.result: Both monotiles form two local-indistinguishability classes (unlike Penrose's single class); the Hat code stores a robust classical bit (handedness) under SE(2) gauge; exact reflected-Hat frequencies are (3∓√5)/6; Spectre orientation-class frequencies are (5±√15)/10; a certified 2490-tile patch retiles uniquely, supporting unconditional local recoverability for nonsingular tilings.
AI.conclusion: The Hat monotile yields a quantum error-correcting code with protected quantum sectors plus a classical chirality bit; the reflexible (Hat) rather than chiral (Spectre) monotile carries the chirality bit; the Spectre's classes merge under all proper isometries, making the classical label vanish.

title: Non-Hermitian Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm
summary: Non-Hermitian systems offer new opportunities for quantum optimization and computation. Here, we show that non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic algorithms require not only a real, gapped spectrum, but also a stable pseudospectrum. We propose a novel framework by mapping non-unitary quantum circuits to local Hamiltonian paths, thereby preserving their optimization advantages and shallow depth. While a direct non-Hermitian extension of the Feynman-Kitaev construction suffers severe pseudospectral instability, our history-decoupled construction yields both a controlled pseudospectrum and a real, gapped spectrum. Using the CK benchmark family of maximum independent set problems, we demonstrate polynomial-evolution-time non-Hermitian adiabatic computation that remains robust against perturbations. We further discuss a feasible optical implementation using coupled waveguides with an auxiliary lossy channel. Our work establishes pseudospectral stability, alongside real, gapped spectra, as key principles and a practical route for non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic computation.

AI.tldr: Non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic algorithms require both a real, gapped spectrum and a stable pseudospectrum. The authors propose a history-decoupled construction that overcomes pseudospectral instability in the direct Feynman-Kitaev extension, enabling polynomial-evolution-time adiabatic computation with robustness against perturbations, demonstrated on maximum independent set problems.
AI.motivation: To establish that pseudospectral stability, alongside real gapped spectra, is a necessary condition for non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic computation, and to provide a practical framework that preserves the optimization advantages of non-Hermitian systems.
AI.method: Mapping non-unitary quantum circuits to local Hamiltonian paths; introducing a history-decoupled construction to replace the unstable direct Feynman-Kitaev approach; testing on the CK benchmark family of maximum independent set problems.
AI.result: The history-decoupled construction yields both a controlled pseudospectrum and a real, gapped spectrum. Non-Hermitian adiabatic computation achieves polynomial evolution time and remains robust against perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Pseudospectral stability is a key principle alongside real, gapped spectra for non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic algorithms. A feasible optical implementation using coupled waveguides with an auxiliary lossy channel is discussed.

title: Causality from the spectrum: Emergence of causal order from process-matrix mereology
summary: In Hamiltonian systems, the only basis-independent quantity is the spectrum. Given a spectrum, quantum mereology seeks preferred tensor-product decompositions into local subsystems, leading to the emergence of locality. Causal order, however, remains fixed by the Hamiltonian time evolution. In contrast, higher-order quantum theory permits more general processes that need not possess a definite global causal order. In the process-matrix framework, specifying a process requires a choice of subsystems corresponding to the input and output Hilbert spaces of each agent. A change of basis redefines both the agents and the corresponding decompositions into subsystems, while leaving the spectrum of the process matrix invariant. Here, we study how causality arises from this spectrum. First, we derive spectral constraints on processes compatible with definite causal order. Second, we show that, in the thermodynamic limit, generic quantum processes admit a preferred decomposition with a definite causal order. This suggests a mechanism for the emergence of classical causality only from algebraic ingredients.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how causal order emerges from the spectrum of process matrices in higher-order quantum theory, showing spectral constraints for definite causal order and that generic quantum processes admit a preferred causally-ordered decomposition in the thermodynamic limit, suggesting classical causality emerges from algebraic ingredients alone.
AI.motivation: To understand how classical causal order emerges from purely algebraic/spectral properties of quantum processes, without assuming any pre-defined causal structure, paralleling how quantum mereology derives locality from spectra in Hamiltonian systems.
AI.method: The authors derive spectral constraints on process matrices compatible with definite causal order, and analyze the thermodynamic limit of generic quantum processes to identify preferred subsystem decompositions that exhibit causal order.
AI.result: Spectral constraints are derived for causally-ordered processes. In the thermodynamic limit, generic quantum processes admit a preferred decomposition with definite causal order, independent of basis choices.
AI.conclusion: Classical causality can emerge from purely algebraic ingredients (the spectrum of the process matrix) without assuming pre-existing causal structure, analogous to how locality emerges in quantum mereology.

title: The Paradox of the Third Particle is classical
summary: The Paradox of the Third Particle arises when particles are described relative to one of them serving as a reference frame. Although it is typically attributed to quantum superpositions, we show that the paradox and its ramifications$\unicode{x2014}$such as the relativity of subsystems$\unicode{x2014}$already occur classically. In light of this insight, we establish a no-go theorem that holds whenever physical subsystems, whether classical or quantum, are used as reference frames: if one demands that frame transformations be information-preserving, then it is impossible to meaningfully partition the world into subsystems, like individual particles, from the perspective of each frame.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the "Paradox of the Third Particle" is a classical phenomenon (not purely quantum), and proves a no-go theorem: if frame transformations must preserve information, then partitioning the world into subsystems (e.g., individual particles) from any reference frame is impossible.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that the Paradox of the Third Particle and its consequences (like relativity of subsystems) are not inherently quantum but already occur classically, and to establish a fundamental limitation on subsystem definitions when using physical reference frames.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis showing the paradox arises classically, followed by a formal no-go theorem applicable to both classical and quantum cases under the condition that frame transformations are information-preserving.
AI.result: The paradox and relativity of subsystems exist classically; a no-go theorem proves that meaningful subsystem partitioning from each frame's perspective is impossible under information-preserving frame transformations.
AI.conclusion: The impossibility of consistent subsystem partitioning is a general feature of using physical subsystems as reference frames, affecting both classical and quantum physics.

title: Spectral amplification for ground-state energy estimation of electronic structure in first quantization
summary: We demonstrate an asymptotic gate complexity improvement in first-quantized ground-state energy estimation of electronic structure Hamiltonians in a plane wave basis by employing the sum-of-squares spectral gap amplification protocol. The improvement relies on identifying a sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian which provides a lower bound certificate and low cost block encoding that leads to a provably lower quantum phase estimation gate cost. This is achieved by using a sum-of-squares operator generated by the total charge density operator resulting in a block encoding normalization improvement of $λ= \mathcal{O}\left(ηΔ^{-1.5}+η^{1.5}Δ^{-1} \right)$ compared to prior work $λ= \mathcal{O}(ηΔ^{-2}+η^2Δ^{-1})$ where $η$ is the number of electrons and $Δ$ is the simulation grid spacing. The asymptotic reduction in block encoding normalization and similar block encoding costs to prior work is demonstrated to reduce resource estimates for materials and chemical systems by a factor of $2 - 44\times$ corresponding to the lowest cost estimates for ab initio materials simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper achieves an asymptotic improvement in the gate complexity for ground-state energy estimation of electronic structure Hamiltonians in a plane wave basis by using the sum-of-squares spectral gap amplification protocol. The key innovation is a sum-of-squares operator derived from the total charge density operator, yielding a better block encoding normalization λ = O(ηΔ^{-1.5} + η^{1.5}Δ^{-1}) compared to prior work's O(ηΔ^{-2} + η^2Δ^{-1}), leading to resource reductions of 2–44× for materials and chemical systems.
AI.motivation: To reduce the quantum gate complexity and resource requirements for ground-state energy estimation of electronic structure Hamiltonians in a plane wave basis, which is a fundamental problem in quantum chemistry and materials science.
AI.method: The authors employ the sum-of-squares spectral gap amplification protocol. They construct a sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian using the total charge density operator, which provides a lower bound certificate and enables low-cost block encoding, yielding an improved normalization factor.
AI.result: The block encoding normalization improves from λ = O(ηΔ^{-2} + η^2Δ^{-1}) (prior work) to λ = O(ηΔ^{-1.5} + η^{1.5}Δ^{-1}). Resource estimates for materials and chemical systems are reduced by a factor of 2–44×, representing the lowest cost estimates for ab initio materials simulation.
AI.conclusion: The sum-of-squares spectral gap amplification protocol with a total charge density operator-based representation provably reduces the asymptotic gate complexity for ground-state energy estimation, enabling more efficient quantum simulations of electronic structure.

title: The Trinity of Markovian Quantum Thermodynamics: Unifying the Axiomatic, Microscopic, and Operational Paradigms
summary: Thermodynamics imposes fundamental constraints on the evolution of quantum systems. These constraints and their dynamical consequences have been formulated within distinct paradigms, including axiomatic approaches based on quantum master equations, microscopic descriptions of open-system dynamics, and operational formulations rooted in resource theories. While each perspective has yielded important insights into thermodynamically consistent quantum dynamics, their precise relationship has remained unresolved. Here we establish the exact equivalence of these three paradigms in the Markovian regime. We prove that thermal Lindbladians satisfying Markovianity, time-translation symmetry, and quantum detailed balance are precisely those admitting a microscopic realisation as an energy-conserving thermal collision model and, equivalently, those generating Markovian thermal operations. This unifies the existing approaches to Markovian quantum thermodynamics and identifies its dynamical underpinnings. We further provide an explicit microscopic protocol for simulating thermal Markovian processes with controlled finite-time simulation errors. We illustrate its applicability by providing faithful thermal collision-model implementations of a qubit thermalising in a bosonic environment and of a three-level autonomous thermal machine. In the latter case, the protocol gives rise to a finite-stroke thermal engine that not only reproduces the continuous-time dynamics but also its steady-state thermodynamic performance. As a whole, these results establish a unified foundation for Markovian quantum thermodynamics, showing that its axiomatic, microscopic, and operational formulations are exactly equivalent and providing a universal protocol for implementing thermal processes and machines.

AI.tldr: This paper proves the exact equivalence of three major paradigms in Markovian quantum thermodynamics—axiomatic master equations, microscopic open-system dynamics, and operational resource theories—by showing thermal Lindbladians with Markovianity, time-translation symmetry, and quantum detailed balance are equivalent to energy-conserving thermal collision models and Markovian thermal operations. It provides a universal simulation protocol with finite-time error bounds and demonstrates applications to qubit thermalization and autonomous thermal machines.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing unresolved relationship between the three distinct paradigms (axiomatic, microscopic, operational) that have been used to formulate thermodynamically consistent quantum dynamics, and to establish whether they are fundamentally equivalent or not.
AI.method: The authors prove rigorous mathematical equivalences: thermal Lindbladians satisfying Markovianity, time-translation symmetry, and quantum detailed balance are exactly those that admit a microscopic realization as an energy-conserving thermal collision model, and equivalently those that generate Markovian thermal operations. They also develop an explicit microscopic protocol for simulating such processes with controlled finite-time simulation errors.
AI.result: The three paradigms are exactly equivalent in the Markovian regime. The authors provide a universal protocol for simulating thermal Markovian processes, demonstrated via qubit thermalization in a bosonic bath and a three-level autonomous thermal machine, where the latter yields a finite-stroke thermal engine reproducing both continuous dynamics and steady-state thermodynamic performance.
AI.conclusion: A unified foundation for Markovian quantum thermodynamics is established, showing axiomatic, microscopic, and operational formulations are exactly equivalent. The work also provides a universal protocol for implementing thermal processes and machines, bridging fundamental theory with practical simulation.

title: Saturating the Bayesian Nagaoka-Hayashi bound within numerical precision for the depolarization SU(2) rotation channel
summary: The Bayesian Nagaoka--Hayashi (NH) bound is a semidefinite lower bound on the Bayes risk of multiparameter estimation, tighter than the Bayesian symmertic logarithmic derivative (SLD) Cramér--Rao bounds, and whether it can be attained is an open problem. We study the single-shot estimation of a qubit rotation, all three parameters at once, under depolarizing noise and a uniform prior, with $k$ parallel uses of the channel. Rotational covariance reduces the joint optimization of probe, measurement, and estimator, and the NH bound itself, to small semidefinite programs, solvable through $k=4$. At every number of uses and noise strength the optimized strategy reaches the NH bound within the numerical precision of the calculation, numerical evidence that the bound is attained for this channel family, while the SLD bound lies strictly below and is never attained. As the noise grows the optimal probe collapses to the tensored Bell state.

AI.tldr: Single-shot estimation of a qubit rotation under depolarizing noise is studied, showing the Bayesian Nagaoka-Hayashi bound is attainable while the SLD bound is not.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the Bayesian Nagaoka-Hayashi (NH) bound, a tighter lower bound than the SLD Cramér-Rao bound for multiparameter estimation, can be attained—an open problem in quantum metrology.
AI.method: Studied single-shot estimation of a qubit rotation (3 parameters) under depolarizing noise with uniform prior and k parallel channel uses. Used rotational covariance to reduce joint optimization of probe, measurement, and estimator, as well as the NH bound, to small semidefinite programs solvable through k=4.
AI.result: At every number of uses and noise strength, the optimized strategy reaches the NH bound within numerical precision, while the SLD bound lies strictly below and is never attained. Optimal probe collapses to tensored Bell state as noise increases.
AI.conclusion: The NH bound is numerically attained for this channel family, providing evidence that the bound can be saturated, whereas the SLD bound cannot.

title: Boosting State Discrimination in Quantum Brownian Motion Channel via Memory-Induced Coherence Preservation
summary: Preserving quantum resources in dissipative environments is a fundamental challenge in quantum information processing. While environmental interactions usually degrade quantum resources, we theoretically show that in a Quantum Brownian Motion (QBM) channel, continuous-variable state discrimination can be improved by increasing, rather than minimizing, the initial thermal noise. Specifically, without suppressing the inherent environmental dissipation, when combined with squeezing, this initial noise induces a coherence preservation mechanism driven by the transient non-thermalization of the probe with the bath. This preservation translates into a pronounced reduction in error probabilities for state discrimination between orthogonal squeezing directions. Furthermore, we also show that quadrature homodyne detection achieves near-optimal performance, approaching the Helstrom limit. These results highlight the advantage of exploiting thermal-squeezed states, offering a robust physical architecture for quantum communication in high-temperature environments.

AI.tldr: In a Quantum Brownian Motion channel, increasing initial thermal noise combined with squeezing can improve continuous-variable state discrimination by preserving coherence via transient non-thermalization, reducing error probabilities and allowing near-optimal homodyne detection.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of preserving quantum resources in dissipative environments, and to explore whether increasing initial thermal noise (rather than minimizing it) can improve state discrimination in a QBM channel.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of a Quantum Brownian Motion channel, using initial thermal noise combined with squeezing to induce a coherence preservation mechanism via transient non-thermalization of the probe with the bath. Performance is evaluated using error probabilities for discriminating orthogonal squeezing directions, and quadrature homodyne detection is compared against the Helstrom limit.
AI.result: Increasing initial thermal noise, when combined with squeezing, reduces error probabilities for state discrimination between orthogonal squeezing directions. Quadrature homodyne detection achieves near-optimal performance, approaching the Helstrom limit.
AI.conclusion: Thermal-squeezed states offer a robust physical architecture for quantum communication in high-temperature environments, demonstrating that environmental noise can be exploited rather than suppressed.

title: Performance Model for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Workflows
summary: Hybrid quantum-classical workflows are expected to underpin practical quantum computing applications, yet the quantum and HPC communities lack a shared framework for reasoning about where and when their integration requirements matter most. Such a framework must separate two distinct levels of analysis: the application level, where communication overhead affects runtime performance, and the real-time level, where it determines feasibility. To address this, we introduce a runtime model that decomposes workflow execution into quantum compute, classical compute, and communication costs. At the application level, a communication-to-computation ratio from this decomposition quantifies whether a workflow is communication-bound or compute-bound; at the real-time level, a feasibility constraint determines whether timing requirements can be met at all, with the reaction time setting the logical clock speed of fault-tolerant computation once they are. Application of this model to representative workflows demonstrates that co-location of quantum processors with HPC infrastructure offers negligible performance benefit for compute-intensive applications today, while tight integration remains crucial for real-time tasks such as quantum error correction needed for large scale quantum computations. However, we discuss how even at the application level these assessments may shift with hardware evolution, illustrating how the model can identify specific crossover conditions, and how, under fault tolerance, the reaction time can set application-level performance.

AI.tldr: Introduces a runtime model for hybrid quantum-classical workflows that separates application-level (communication vs. compute bound) and real-time level (feasibility via reaction time) analysis, showing co-location benefits real-time tasks like error correction but not compute-bound applications today.
AI.motivation: Quantum and HPC communities lack a shared framework to reason about where and when integration requirements (e.g., co-location, tight coupling) matter for hybrid quantum-classical workflows.
AI.method: A runtime model decomposing workflow execution into quantum compute, classical compute, and communication costs. Application-level uses a communication-to-computation ratio to classify workflows; real-time level uses a feasibility constraint with reaction time setting logical clock speed for fault-tolerant computation.
AI.result: Co-location offers negligible performance benefit for today's compute-intensive applications, but tight integration remains crucial for real-time tasks like quantum error correction. The model identifies crossover conditions where these assessments shift with hardware evolution.
AI.conclusion: The model provides a structured way to analyze integration requirements across two levels, showing that reaction time under fault tolerance can set application-level performance, and that future hardware changes may shift the communication vs. compute balance.

title: Generation and detection of squeezed light on a single silicon photonic chip
summary: The ability to generate and detect quantum states of light on a single integrated photonic device is essential to scale quantum photonics into useful quantum technologies. Integrating the required capabilities into complementary-metal-oxide-semiconductor compatible monolithic chips can reduce cost and unlock new functionality through miniaturisation. In this work we demonstrate a single silicon-on-insulator photonic integrated circuit for the monolithic generation and detection of quantum light on a commercially available platform that operates entirely at room temperature. Specifically, we leverage spontaneous four-wave mixing in silicon waveguides to produce squeezed light which is subsequently detected by photodiodes operating in a pulsed homodyne detector configuration on the same chip as the source. We directly measure $0.25(1)$ dB of squeezing, including contributions from waveguide propagation loss and detection inefficiency, and include a detailed analysis of the impact of nonlinear loss on the squeezing levels achievable using this platform.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a silicon-on-insulator photonic integrated circuit that monolithically generates and detects squeezed light at room temperature, achieving 0.25 dB of squeezing using spontaneous four-wave mixing and on-chip pulsed homodyne detection.
AI.motivation: Scaling quantum photonics into practical quantum technologies requires the integration of quantum light generation and detection on a single chip. Reducing cost and unlocking new functionality through miniaturization and CMOS-compatible fabrication motivates this work.
AI.method: A monolithic silicon-on-insulator photonic integrated circuit is used, leveraging spontaneous four-wave mixing in silicon waveguides to generate squeezed light, which is then detected by on-chip photodiodes in a pulsed homodyne detector configuration, all operating at room temperature.
AI.result: Direct measurement of 0.25(1) dB of squeezing, accounting for waveguide propagation loss and detection inefficiency. A detailed analysis of nonlinear loss impact on squeezing levels is also provided.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates a commercially viable, room-temperature platform for monolithic quantum light generation and detection on a single chip, advancing scalability of quantum photonic technologies.

title: Efficient routing and spectrum allocation in arbitrary flex-grid entanglement networks
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 1 table; submitted to Optics Express
summary: As practical quantum networks approach large-scale deployment, the need for efficient user-to-user frequency allocation is increasing, yet current approaches only provide partial solutions to the routing and spectrum allocation problem for an arbitrary quantum network. We address this challenge for repeater-less flex-grid quantum networks based on hyperentangled photons using an efficient three-stage pipeline combining leading tools in classical networking with recent advances in numerical optimization. First, double instantiations of Yen's algorithm obtain low-loss route candidates between each pair of users and the entanglement sources. Second, the advanced process optimizer (APOPT) obtains frequency channel allocations that maximize distribution rates under fidelity constraints. Finally, the constraint programming solver using satisfiability methods (CP-SAT) assigns specific frequency bins to each link, ensuring that there is no contention between frequencies from different sources. We numerically demonstrate this approach on a representative ring network and a Manhattan incumbent local exchange carrier topology, realizing significant improvements over prior genetic algorithm approaches in speed, accuracy, and scalability. Overall, this pipeline provides an efficient heuristic workflow for optimizing broadband entanglement distribution, applicable to arbitrarily connected quantum networks integrated within the existing lightwave infrastructure.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a three-stage pipeline combining Yen's algorithm, APOPT optimizer, and CP-SAT solver for routing and spectrum allocation in repeater-less flex-grid quantum networks using hyperentangled photons, demonstrating significant improvements in speed, accuracy, and scalability over prior genetic algorithm approaches on ring and Manhattan topologies.
AI.motivation: As practical quantum networks approach large-scale deployment, existing approaches only provide partial solutions to the routing and spectrum allocation problem for arbitrary quantum networks, motivating the need for a comprehensive solution.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) Double instantiations of Yen's algorithm obtain low-loss route candidates between users and entanglement sources; (2) APOPT optimizer obtains frequency channel allocations maximizing distribution rates under fidelity constraints; (3) CP-SAT solver assigns specific frequency bins to each link to prevent contention.
AI.result: Numerical demonstration on a ring network and Manhattan incumbent local exchange carrier topology shows significant improvements over prior genetic algorithm approaches in speed, accuracy, and scalability.
AI.conclusion: This pipeline provides an efficient heuristic workflow for optimizing broadband entanglement distribution, applicable to arbitrarily connected quantum networks integrated within existing lightwave infrastructure.

title: The Complexity of Dynamical Correlators: Operator Shadows and Exponential Learning Separations
summary: Quantum platforms can realize many-body dynamics beyond classical simulation yet complete readout remains intractable: the cost of extracting accessible information scales exponentially with system size. Classical shadows and Bell sampling offer scalable, multi-observable estimation from randomized or entanglement-assisted measurements. Here we aim to push these ideas beyond static snapshots to dynamical correlators, including out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) and two-point functions. In particular, we introduce the notion of the shadow of an operator, defined as the classical shadow of the vectorized time-evolved operator. Pauli operator-shadows enable simultaneous estimation of all local OTOCs, while Clifford operator-shadows enable efficient simultaneous estimation of all two-point correlators. Alternatively, Bell sampling allows one to simultaneously compute all diagonal OTOCs. We also prove information-theoretic lower bounds for learning OTOCs, fully characterizing their query complexities in many cases, and yielding exponential separations that formalize when the vectorized approach provides measurement-efficiency advantages.

AI.tldr: This paper extends classical shadows and Bell sampling techniques from static observable estimation to dynamical correlators (OTOCs and two-point functions), introducing operator-shadows (Pauli and Clifford) and vectorized time-evolved operators to enable scalable, simultaneous estimation of these quantities, backed by information-theoretic lower bounds and exponential advantage proofs.
AI.motivation: Complete readout of quantum many-body dynamics is intractable due to exponential scaling; the paper aims to extend scalable randomized/entanglement-assisted measurement schemes (classical shadows, Bell sampling) from static snapshots to dynamical correlators like OTOCs and two-point functions.
AI.method: Introduces the "shadow of an operator" via vectorized time-evolved operator classical shadows. Uses Pauli operator-shadows for all local OTOCs, Clifford operator-shadows for all two-point correlators, and Bell sampling for all diagonal OTOCs. Derives information-theoretic lower bounds to characterize query complexity.
AI.result: Pauli operator-shadows enable simultaneous estimation of all local OTOCs; Clifford operator-shadows enable simultaneous estimation of all two-point correlators; Bell sampling computes all diagonal OTOCs simultaneously. Information-theoretic lower bounds yield exponential separations, formalizing regimes where the vectorized approach provides measurement-efficiency advantages.
AI.conclusion: Classical shadows and Bell sampling can be successfully extended to dynamical correlators, offering scalable measurement protocols for OTOCs and two-point functions, with provable exponential advantages in certain regimes.

title: Microscopic Side Information Controls Ordered Hayden--Preskill Recovery
summary: In the Hayden--Preskill protocol, the decoder is usually assumed to know the microscopic identity of the collected output qubits. We study what happens when these labels are unavailable and only the relative order of the received qubits is preserved. The resulting order-preserving deletion channel maps an $n$-qubit scrambled register to a subsequence of length $\ell$. For a diary of fixed size $k$, we prove that the optimal entanglement fidelity converges to the no-output value $4^{-k}$ when $\ell=o(n^{2/3})$, uniformly over the scrambling unitary. For a Haar-random scrambling unitary, it converges to one when $\ell=ω(n^{2/3})$ and $\ell=o(n)$. Monotonicity then gives the fixed-error recovery scale $\ell_{\mathrm{rec}}=Θ(n^{2/3})$. We also consider partial position information obtained by dividing the register into $B$ consecutive blocks and revealing the block of origin of each received qubit. The recovery scale becomes $\ell_{\mathrm{rec}}(n,B)\asymp n^{2/3}B^{-1/3}$ for $B\leq\sqrt n$ and $\ell_{\mathrm{rec}}(n,B)\asymp n/B$ for $B\geq\sqrt n$. The exponent $2/3$ is traced to rank-aligned coincidences between random subsequences, which control both the converse and the recovery argument. Thus, even purely classical information about the origin of the received subsystems can change the amount of quantum output required for Hayden--Preskill recovery.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the Hayden-Preskill protocol when qubit labels are unavailable, only preserving order. It finds optimal entanglement fidelity transitions at ℓ ~ n^{2/3}, establishing the recovery scale ℓ_rec = Θ(n^{2/3}) for the order-preserving deletion channel. Partial block information modifies this scale to ℓ_rec(n,B) ≍ n^{2/3}B^{-1/3} (B≤√n) or n/B (B≥√n).
AI.motivation: To understand Hayden-Preskill recovery when the decoder lacks microscopic identity labels of collected output qubits, only preserving their relative order—a more realistic scenario.
AI.method: Analyzes the order-preserving deletion channel; proves entanglement fidelity convergence bounds for fixed-size diary and Haar-random scrambling unitary; uses rank-aligned coincidences between random subsequences to derive recovery scales.
AI.result: Optimal entanglement fidelity converges to 4^{-k} for ℓ=o(n^{2/3}) and to 1 for ℓ=ω(n^{2/3}) with ℓ=o(n). Recovery scale ℓ_rec=Θ(n^{2/3}). With partial block information, ℓ_rec(n,B) ≍ n^{2/3}B^{-1/3} for B≤√n and ℓ_rec(n,B) ≍ n/B for B≥√n.
AI.conclusion: Even classical information about subsystem origin affects quantum output requirements for Hayden-Preskill recovery. The exponent 2/3 is fundamental, arising from rank-aligned coincidences in random subsequences.

title: Benchmarking Hybrid Quantum-Classical Algorithms for Power Grid Optimization Problems
summary: Alternating Current Optimal Power Flow Unit Commitment (AC-OPF-UC) is a difficult mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problem that combines binary generator commitment decisions with nonconvex continuous AC power-flow constraints. In this work, we investigate whether hybrid quantum-classical variational algorithms can improve the solution of single-period AC-OPF-UC relative to classical approaches. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to directly evaluate quantum or hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for the full AC-OPF-UC problem. We consider two candidate algorithms for improving AC-OPF-UC solution quality relative to purely classical methods on ideal quantum hardware. The first applies QAOA directly to a fully discretized formulation of the problem, with equality and inequality constraints incorporated through penalty terms and slack variables. Although conceptually straightforward, this approach requires a prohibitively large number of qubits even for small instances. The second, qubit-efficient approach encodes only the binary generator status variables on a quantum computer, while optimizing the continuous power-flow variables classically for each sampled bitstring. We benchmark this method on randomly generated AC-OPF-UC instances with 5 to 13 generators and compare it against SCIP, SMAC, and uniform random sampling. Our simulations show that the qubit-efficient hybrid method does not outperform uniform sampling. These results suggest that in order to establish potential advantage of the variational hybrid strategy considered here over the best classical algorithms, if any, much larger system sizes (25+ generators) need to be tested, which is beyond our computational capacity. Alternatively, different approaches, such as quantum versions of branch-and-bound methods, may be more promising.

AI.tldr: This study investigates hybrid quantum-classical variational algorithms for the AC-OPF-UC problem. Two approaches are examined: a QAOA-based fully discretized method (requiring too many qubits) and a qubit-efficient hybrid method encoding only binary variables. Benchmarks on 5–13 generator instances show the hybrid method does not outperform uniform random sampling. The authors conclude that much larger systems (25+ generators) or alternative quantum approaches (e.g., quantum branch-and-bound) may be needed to demonstrate potential advantage.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether hybrid quantum-classical variational algorithms can improve the solution of single-period AC-OPF-UC relative to classical approaches, as this is the first study to directly assess such algorithms for the full AC-OPF-UC problem.
AI.method: Two candidate algorithms were considered: (1) QAOA applied to a fully discretized formulation with penalty terms and slack variables (conceptually straightforward but requiring a prohibitive number of qubits); (2) a qubit-efficient hybrid approach where only binary generator status variables are encoded on a quantum computer while continuous power-flow variables are optimized classically for each sampled bitstring. Benchmarks were conducted on randomly generated instances with 5–13 generators against SCIP, SMAC, and uniform random sampling.
AI.result: The qubit-efficient hybrid method did not outperform uniform random sampling on instances with 5–13 generators. The fully discretized QAOA approach was infeasible due to excessive qubit requirements even for small instances.
AI.conclusion: To potentially demonstrate advantage over classical algorithms, much larger system sizes (25+ generators) need to be tested, which is beyond current computational capacity. Alternatively, different quantum approaches (e.g., quantum versions of branch-and-bound methods) may be more promising.

title: Quantum states supported by matroids
comment: This paper has been published in Physical Review A. Commements are welcome
summary: In this work, we establish a structural correspondence between quantum states and matroid theory. This connection demonstrates that key properties of quantum states, including entanglement and measurement, can be characterized in purely combinatorial terms via matroids, despite the apparent conceptual distance between these two fields. Using this framework, we show that a matroid-supported state is genuinely entangled when its underlying matroid is connected. Moreover, a uniform superposition over all bases of a matroid is genuinely entangled if and only if the matroid is connected. We also demonstrate that a local measurement in the $Z$-basis on such a state yields another matroid-supported state, whose underlying matroid is a minor of the original one. Inspired by matroid duality, we further propose a notion of quantum state duality, uncovering a deep structural symmetry in state transformations.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a formal correspondence between quantum states and matroid theory, showing that entanglement and measurement can be characterized combinatorially, and introduces a notion of quantum state duality inspired by matroid duality.
AI.motivation: To bridge the conceptual gap between quantum information theory and combinatorial matroid theory by demonstrating that key quantum properties (entanglement, measurement) can be characterized in purely combinatorial terms.
AI.method: The paper develops a structural correspondence between quantum states and matroids, analyzing conditions for genuine entanglement via matroid connectivity, examining uniform superpositions over matroid bases, studying Z-basis measurements as matroid minors, and proposing a duality notion inspired by matroid duality.
AI.result: A matroid-supported state is genuinely entangled iff its underlying matroid is connected; a uniform superposition over all bases of a matroid is genuinely entangled iff the matroid is connected; a Z-basis measurement yields another matroid-supported state whose matroid is a minor of the original.
AI.conclusion: Matroid theory provides a powerful combinatorial framework for characterizing quantum state properties, with matroid duality leading to a novel notion of quantum state duality that reveals deep structural symmetries in state transformations.

title: Agnostic learning of qudit stabilizer states
summary: Learning a classical description of a quantum state is a fundamental task in quantum computation. Among the most important classes of quantum states are stabilizer states, which play a central role in quantum error correction and fault-tolerant computation. To mitigate the effects of realistic noise, agnostic learning of stabilizer states has emerged as a natural and well-motivated problem. Recently, Chen \textit{et al.} [STOC'25, p. 429-438] resolved this problem for qubit systems by using a stabilizer bootstrapping framework. However, the agnostic learning of qudit stabilizer states remains largely unexplored, since the qudit setting introduces fundamental structural differences that prevent a direct generalization of existing qubit techniques. In this paper, we successfully generalize the stabilizer bootstrapping framework to qudit systems and present the first efficient quantum algorithm for agnostic learning of qudit stabilizer states. Specifically, given copies of an unknown $n$-qudit pure state $|ψ\rangle$ that has fidelity $τ$ with some stabilizer state, our algorithm outputs a stabilizer state $|φ\rangle$ such that $\left| \braket{φ|ψ} \right|^2 \geq τ- \varepsilon$ with high probability. The algorithm uses only single-copy and four-copy measurements, and its sample and time complexity scale as $(d/τ)^{O(d^2 \log(1/τ))} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(n, 1/\varepsilon)$, where the dimension $d$ is an odd prime. As a direct corollary, our algorithm enables efficient estimation of the magic of a quantum state, as quantified by its stabilizer fidelity. Completing the picture, we also present a streamlined algorithm for the high-fidelity regime $τ> \cos^2(π/8)$, establishing a qudit analogue of the threshold-based approach in prior qubit work.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first efficient quantum algorithm for agnostically learning qudit stabilizer states by generalizing the stabilizer bootstrapping framework from qubits to qudits (odd prime dimension d). The algorithm uses single-copy and four-copy measurements, achieves sample/time complexity scaling as $(d/τ)^{O(d^2 \log(1/τ))} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(n, 1/\varepsilon)$, and enables efficient estimation of magic (stabilizer fidelity). It also provides a streamlined algorithm for the high-fidelity regime $τ> \cos^2(π/8)$.
AI.motivation: Agnostic learning of stabilizer states is important for quantum error correction and fault-tolerant computation under realistic noise. While the qubit case was recently resolved, the qudit setting remained unexplored due to fundamental structural differences that prevent direct generalization of qubit techniques.
AI.method: Generalizes the stabilizer bootstrapping framework to qudit systems (odd prime dimension d). Uses only single-copy and four-copy measurements. For the high-fidelity regime $τ > \cos^2(π/8)$, a streamlined threshold-based algorithm is also provided.
AI.result: The algorithm outputs a stabilizer state $|φ\rangle$ with fidelity $\left| \braket{φ|ψ} \right|^2 \geq τ- \varepsilon$ with high probability. Sample and time complexity: $(d/τ)^{O(d^2 \log(1/τ))} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(n, 1/\varepsilon)$. Also enables efficient estimation of magic via stabilizer fidelity.
AI.conclusion: This work resolves the agnostic learning problem for qudit stabilizer states, establishing a qudit analogue of prior qubit results and completing the picture with a high-fidelity regime algorithm.

title: Deterministic atom-shuttle interconnects via ultrafast atom-ion entangling gate
summary: Neutral-atom arrays and trapped-ion crystals offer complementary strengths for fault-tolerant quantum computing but lack a fast way to deterministically interact. Here we propose a controlled-$Z$ gate generated by the charge-induced-dipole ($C_4$) force between a Rydberg-excited atom and a trapped ion, balanced by a spin-dependent optical Magnus force on the ion that closes phase-space trajectories within a few microseconds. Toggling the Rydberg state extends the scheme to multi-ion crystals at negligible overhead. The resulting ${\sim}5\,$kHz atom shuttle accelerates short-distance QCCD links and enables hybrid qLDPC memories in which atom logical qubits are written onto an ion block treated as a passive storage zone. We perform circuit-level Monte Carlo simulations and find that the hybrid architecture supports orders of magnitude more operations than atom-only or ion-only architectures at fixed code distance and logical error rate.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hybrid quantum computing architecture combining neutral atoms and trapped ions using a C4 force-based controlled-Z gate, enabling fast inter-species interaction and significantly outperforming homogeneous architectures in circuit-level Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.motivation: Neutral-atom arrays and trapped-ion crystals have complementary strengths for fault-tolerant quantum computing but currently lack a fast, deterministic method for inter-species interaction.
AI.method: A controlled-Z gate is generated via charge-induced-dipole (C4) force between a Rydberg-excited atom and a trapped ion, balanced by a spin-dependent optical Magnus force on the ion. Toggling the Rydberg state extends the scheme to multi-ion crystals.
AI.result: The atom shuttle achieves ~5 kHz speed for short-distance QCCD links. Circuit-level Monte Carlo simulations show the hybrid architecture supports orders of magnitude more operations than atom-only or ion-only architectures at fixed code distance and logical error rate.
AI.conclusion: This hybrid approach enables fast, scalable inter-species gates and supports hybrid qLDPC memories where atom logical qubits are written onto passive ion storage zones, outperforming homogeneous alternatives.

title: Classical codes violate the conjectured square-root bound for quantum random access codes
summary: We consider whether every quantum random access code (QRAC) with density-operator encodings and arbitrary decoding measurements obeys the conjectured bound $p\leq(1+\sqrt{m/n})/2$, where $n$ classical bits are encoded into $m$ qubits and $p$ is the worst-case success probability. We find that classical random access codes with private randomness, which form a subclass of this QRAC model, violate the bound. We embed these classical codes as QRACs with diagonal encoding states and commuting decoding measurements, and construct pure-state realizations with identical decoding statistics. The achievability theorem of Ambainis, Nayak, Ta-Shma, and Vazirani then yields violations for every fixed $p\in(1/2,1)$ at sufficiently large input length. The counterexamples span the full open interval between the conjectured and Nayak bounds at each fixed compression rate. A finite-blocklength analysis further yields order-optimal logarithmic qubit scaling for a recovery bias scaling as $\sqrt{\log_2 n/n}$ with a sufficiently large prefactor. These results identify the classical coding rate as the source of the separation and motivate restricted bounds based on quantitative spectral properties of decoding measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper disproves a conjectured bound on quantum random access codes by showing that classical random access codes with private randomness violate it, and constructs explicit violations across the full range between the conjectured and Nayak bounds.
AI.motivation: To test the validity of a conjectured bound $p \leq (1+\sqrt{m/n})/2$ for quantum random access codes (QRACs) with density-operator encodings and arbitrary decoding measurements, which would be a stronger constraint than the known Nayak bound.
AI.method: The authors identify that classical random access codes with private randomness form a subclass of the considered QRAC model, embed them as QRACs with diagonal encoding states and commuting decoding measurements, construct pure-state realizations with identical statistics, and apply the achievability theorem of Ambainis et al. to produce counterexamples.
AI.result: Violations of the conjectured bound are found for every fixed success probability $p \in (1/2,1)$ at sufficiently large input length, spanning the full open interval between the conjectured and Nayak bounds. Finite-blocklength analysis yields order-optimal logarithmic qubit scaling for recovery bias scaling as $\sqrt{\log_2 n/n}$ with large prefactor.
AI.conclusion: The classical coding rate is identified as the source of the separation between the conjectured bound and the Nayak bound, motivating future restricted bounds based on quantitative spectral properties of decoding measurements.

title: Fate of dynamical quantum phase transitions from sudden quench to slow quench limit
summary: Previous investigations of dynamical quantum phase transition (DQPT) have predominantly focused on sudden quench protocols. In this work, we systematically explore the fate of DQPT from the sudden to the slow quench regime. We establish that DQPT remains robust under slow quenching when the protocol crosses an equilibrium quantum phase transition. Conversely, we show that accidental DQPTs,which occur when the pre and post quench Hamiltonians reside in the same equilibrium phase, can be filtered out in the slow quench limit. This demonstrates that slow quenches can reveal the intrinsic connection between DQPT and equilibrium quantum phase transitions, thereby enabling DQPT to serve as a dynamical probe for identifying equilibrium quantum critical points. We illustrate these findings with examples from the XY chain, the Aubry-André model, and the trimer Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPT) remain robust under slow quenches when crossing an equilibrium quantum phase transition, but accidental DQPTs (occurring within the same phase) are filtered out, revealing the intrinsic connection between DQPT and equilibrium quantum critical points.
AI.motivation: Previous studies of DQPT focused mainly on sudden quench protocols, leaving the slow quench regime and the connection between DQPT and equilibrium quantum phase transitions largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors systematically investigate DQPT from sudden to slow quench regimes, analyzing its behavior when crossing vs. not crossing equilibrium quantum phase transitions, using examples from the XY chain, Aubry-André model, and trimer Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model.
AI.result: DQPT persists under slow quenching when the protocol crosses an equilibrium quantum phase transition, while accidental DQPTs (occurring within the same equilibrium phase) vanish in the slow quench limit.
AI.conclusion: Slow quenches can reveal the intrinsic connection between DQPT and equilibrium quantum phase transitions, allowing DQPT to serve as a dynamical probe for identifying equilibrium quantum critical points.

title: Spectral Attack on Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution Systems
summary: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) has attracted extensive attention due to its compatibility and low costs. However, bandwidth mismatch exists to varying degrees between the transmitter and receiver. This may prevent frequency components carrying modulation information from being fully perceived by the legitimate party. In this paper, we identify a practical security loophole caused by bandwidth mismatch and propose a corresponding spectral attack scheme. Different from previous approaches that exploit security loopholes to conceal the excess noise introduced by intercept-resend attacks, this scheme can directly obtain raw-key information without introducing additional disturbances. A proof-of-principle attack on a CVQKD system with filtering operation is constructed to verify the feasibility. Experimental results indicate that Eve can obtain enough information to render the system insecure if this practical security loophole is ignored. Based on the identified security loophole, corresponding defense strategies are proposed. This work helps bridge the gap between theoretical models and practical implementations, providing a reference for defense design in practical quantum communication systems.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a practical security loophole in CVQKD systems caused by bandwidth mismatch between transmitter and receiver, proposes a spectral attack that directly extracts raw-key information without introducing disturbances, and demonstrates experimentally that such an attack can compromise system security.
AI.motivation: Bandwidth mismatch between transmitter and receiver in CVQKD systems may prevent legitimate parties from fully perceiving frequency components carrying modulation information, creating a potential security loophole that needs to be identified and addressed to bridge the gap between theoretical security models and practical implementations.
AI.method: The authors identify the bandwidth mismatch security loophole and propose a spectral attack scheme that directly obtains raw-key information without introducing additional disturbances (unlike conventional intercept-resend attacks that conceal excess noise). A proof-of-principle attack on a CVQKD system with filtering operation is constructed to verify feasibility.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that Eve can obtain enough information to render the system insecure if the bandwidth mismatch security loophole is ignored. Defense strategies are also proposed.
AI.conclusion: This work helps bridge the gap between theoretical models and practical implementations, providing a reference for defense design in practical quantum communication systems.

title: Boundary-Phase Control of Sequentially Addressed Trapped-Ion ZZ Interactions
comment: Main text: 6 figures. Supplementary Information included
summary: Motion-mediated trapped-ion gates typically apply synchronized state-dependent forces to both target ions. We consider the complementary setting in which one addressing channel alternates between the targets, so their force windows do not overlap. In a complex-amplitude near-resonant description, each window generates a displacement vector, and ordered symplectic products of vectors on different ions produce the ZZ phase. For fixed envelopes and timings, relative rotations of the window displacement vectors redirect the sign and magnitude of this phase, whereas a common rotation of all displacement vectors leaves the pair phase invariant. Motivated by experimental alternating-addressing protocols, we design matched-envelope phase and contrast controls that distinguish the boundary-phase response from closure error and residual force in dark gaps. Waveform synthesis suppresses differential motion, while a reduced-spin map that is exact within the linear spin-dependent-force model accounts for projector-common motion, deterministic local-Z phases, spectator coupling, and control-parameter drift. A conditional-Ramsey protocol predicts continuous and reset contrasts of 0.998 and 0.996, with the reset rule redirecting the extracted pair phase by 0.581 rad relative to the continuous rule, modulo pi/2. In the representative comparison, sequential control uses only one active target channel at a time, but requires 1.826 times the normalized squared-force action of independently calibrated simultaneous control. For representative experimental parameters and within the stated approximations, the inter-window force-quadrature reference therefore provides an experimentally testable control resource for sequential trapped-ion interactions.

AI.tldr: This paper explores sequential (non-overlapping) state-dependent forces for trapped-ion gates, where alternating addressing windows generate ZZ phases via ordered symplectic products. It designs matched-envelope controls, uses a reduced-spin map for error modeling, and demonstrates high-fidelity conditional-Ramsey contrasts (0.998/0.996) while comparing sequential vs. simultaneous control performance.
AI.motivation: To understand and leverage the complementary regime of alternating (non-overlapping) force windows for trapped-ion entangling gates, moving beyond the standard synchronized-force paradigm, and to identify the experimental utility of inter-window force-quadrature references.
AI.method: Complex-amplitude near-resonant description; matched-envelope phase and contrast controls; reduced-spin map exact within linear spin-dependent-force model; waveform synthesis for differential motion suppression; conditional-Ramsey protocol for contrast prediction.
AI.result: Conditional-Ramsey protocol yields continuous contrast 0.998 and reset contrast 0.996; reset rule redirects extracted pair phase by 0.581 rad vs. continuous rule modulo pi/2; sequential control requires 1.826x the normalized squared-force action of simultaneous control.
AI.conclusion: The inter-window force-quadrature reference provides an experimentally testable control resource for sequential trapped-ion interactions within the stated approximations and representative experimental parameters.

title: Non-Gaussianity in cat codes: global incompatibility and local geometric alignment with the magic resource
summary: Non-Gaussianity is an essential resource for genuine quantum advantages in continuous-variable quantum systems and is regarded as a counterpart of the magic resource in discrete-variable systems. Recently, an exact correspondence between non-Gaussianity (NG) and the magic resource was identified within the Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) encoding framework. Whether such a relation persists beyond GKP encoding, however, remains unclear. Here, we address this question in the cat-code setting. By comparing the Wigner logarithmic negativity (WLN) and a magic measure defined from a phase-operator basis, we analyze the resource geometry of non-degenerate $d$-peaked cat states. We find that cat codes do not inherit the global value-preserving GKP magic--NG equivalence, but their asymptotic WLN geometry allows a constructive local alignment with the magic-measure geometry. Specifically, under a distinguished SU($d$) asymptotic cat code, we establish a sector-dependent alignment between WLN level sets and magic-measure level sets based on their intrinsic local geometries.
